entries.5a3605c9d5de8d15ce08e3bee77d0a68983bf599: <div sID="gen15929" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="Isa.22" sID="Isa.22"/> <div eID="gen15929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15930" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15931" type="x-p"/> We have now come nearer home, for this chapter is "the burden of the valley of vision," Jerusalem; other places had their burden for the sake of their being concerned in some way or other with Jerusalem, and were reckoned with either as spiteful enemies or deceitful friends to the people of God; but now let Jerusalem hear her own doom. This chapter concerns, I. The city of Jerusalem itself and the neighbourhood depending upon it. Here is, 1. A prophecy of the grievous distress they should shortly be brought into by Sennacherib's invasion of the country and laying siege to the city, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.1-Isa.22.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. 2. A reproof given them for their misconduct in that distress, in two things:—(1.) Not having an eye to God in the use of the means of their preservation, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.11">ver. 8-11</reference>. (2.) Not humbling themselves under his mighty hand, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.14">ver. 12-14</reference>. II. The court of Hezekiah, and the officers of that court. 1. The displacing of Shebna, a bad man, and turning him out of the treasury, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.15-Isa.22.19">ver. 15-19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.25">25</reference>. 2. The preferring of Eliakim, who should do his country better service, to his place, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.20-Isa.22.24">ver. 20-24</reference>.
entries.b592c0103a4740d092a4acab80828a3cc0216271: <div eID="gen15931" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15930" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Consternation of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15932" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The burden of the valley of vision. What aileth thee now, that thou art wholly gone up to the housetops? <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou that art full of stirs, a tumultuous city, a joyous city: thy slain <hi type="italic">men are</hi> not slain with the sword, nor dead in battle. <hi type="super">3</hi> All thy rulers are fled together, they are bound by the archers: all that are found in thee are bound together, <hi type="italic">which</hi> have fled from far. <hi type="super">4</hi> Therefore said I, Look away from me; I will weep bitterly, labour not to comfort me, because of the spoiling of the daughter of my people. <hi type="super">5</hi> For <hi type="italic">it is</hi> a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity by the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts in the valley of vision, breaking down the walls, and of crying to the mountains. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Elam bare the quiver with chariots of men <hi type="italic">and</hi> horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. <hi type="super">7</hi> And it shall come to pass, <hi type="italic">that</hi> thy choicest valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall set themselves in array at the gate. <div eID="gen15932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15933" type="x-p"/> The title of this prophecy is very observable. It is <hi type="italic">the burden of the valley of vision,</hi> of Judah and Jerusalem; so all agree. Fitly enough is Jerusalem called a valley, for the mountains were round about it, and the land of Judah abounded with fruitful valleys; and by the judgments of God, though they had been as a towering mountain, they should be brought low, sunk and depressed, and become dark and dirty, as a valley. But most emphatically is it called a <hi type="italic">valley of vision</hi> because there God was known and his name was great, there the prophets were made acquainted with his mind by visions, and there the people saw the goings of their God and King in his sanctuary. Babylon, being a stranger to God, though rich and great, was called <hi type="italic">the desert of the sea;</hi> but Jerusalem, being entrusted with his oracles, is <hi type="italic">a valley of vision. Blessed are their eyes, for they see,</hi> and they have seers by office among them. Where Bibles and ministers are there is a valley of vision, from which is expected fruit accordingly; but here is a <hi type="italic">burden of the valley of vision,</hi> and a heavy burden it is. Note, Church privileges, if they be not improved, will not secure men from the judgments of God. <hi type="italic">You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore will I punish you.</hi> The valley of vision has a particular burden. <hi type="italic">Thou Capernaum,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.23">Matt. xi. 23</reference>. The higher any are lifted up in means and mercies the heavier will their doom be if they abuse them. <div eID="gen15933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15934" type="x-p"/> Now the <hi type="italic">burden of the valley of vision</hi> here is that which will not quite ruin it, but only frighten it; for it refers not to the destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, but to the attempt made upon it by Sennacherib, which we had the prophecy of, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.1-Isa.10.34">ch. x.</reference>, and shall meet with the history of, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1-Isa.36.22">ch. xxxvi.</reference>. It is here again prophesied of, because the desolations of many of the neighbouring countries, which were foretold in the foregoing chapters, were to be brought to pass by the Assyrian army. Now let Jerusalem know that when the cup is going round it will be put into her hand; and, although it will not be to her a fatal cup, yet it will be a cup of trembling. Here is foretold, <div eID="gen15934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15935" type="x-p"/> I. The consternation that the city should be in upon the approach of Sennacherib's army. It used to be full of stirs, a city of great trade, people hurrying to and fro about their business, a tumultuous city, populous and noisy. Where there is great trade there is great tumult. It used to be a joyous revelling city. What with the busy part and what with the merry part of mankind, places of concourse are places of noise. "But what ails thee now, that the shops are quitted, and there is no more walking in the streets and exchange, <hi type="italic">but thou hast wholly gone up to the house-tops</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.1">v. 1</reference>), to bemoan thyself in silence and solitude, or to secure thyself from the enemy, or to look abroad and see if any succours come to thy relief, or which way the enemies' motions are." Let both men of business and sportsmen <hi type="italic">rejoice as though they rejoiced not,</hi> for something may happen quickly, which they little think of, that will be a damp to their mirth and a stop to their business, and send them to <hi type="italic">watch as a sparrow alone upon the house-top,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.7">Ps. cii. 7</reference>. But why is Jerusalem in such a fright? <hi type="italic">Her slain men are not slain with the sword</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">v. 2</reference>), but, 1. Slain with famine (so some); for Sennacherib's army having laid the country waste, and destroyed the fruits of the earth, provisions must needs be very scarce and dear in the city, which would be the death of many of the poorer sort of people, who would be constrained to feed on that which was unwholesome. 2. Slain with fear. They were put into this fright though they had not a man killed, but so disheartened themselves that they seemed as effectually stabbed with fear as if they had been run through with a sword. <div eID="gen15935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15936" type="x-p"/> II. The inglorious flight of the rulers of Judah, who fled from far, from all parts of the country, to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">v. 3</reference>), fled together, as it were by consent, and were found in Jerusalem, having left their respective cities, which they should have taken care of, to be a prey to the Assyrian army, which, meeting with no opposition, when it <hi type="italic">came up against all the defenced cities of Judah</hi> easily <hi type="italic">took them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">ch. xxxvi. 1</reference>. These rulers <hi type="italic">were bound from the bow</hi> (so the word is); they not only quitted their own cities like cowards, but, when they came to Jerusalem, were of no service there, but were as if their hands were tied from the use of the bow, by the extreme distraction and confusion they were in; they trembled, so that they could not draw a bow. See how easily God can dispirit men, and how certainly fear will dispirit them, when the tyranny of it is yielded to. <div eID="gen15936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15937" type="x-p"/> III. The great grief which this should occasion to all serious sensible people among them, which is represented by the prophet's laying the thing to heart himself; he lived to see it, and was resolved to share with the children of his people in their sorrows, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.4-Isa.22.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. He is not willing to proclaim his sorrow, and therefore bids those about him to look away from him; he will abandon himself to grief, and indulge himself in it, will weep secretly, but weep bitterly, and will have none go about to comfort him, for his grief is obstinate and he is pleased with his pain. But what is the occasion of his grief? A poor prophet had little to lose, and had been inured to hardship, when he walked naked and barefoot; but it is for <hi type="italic">the spoiling of the daughter of his people.</hi> It is <hi type="italic">a day of trouble, and of treading down, and of perplexity.</hi> Our enemies trouble us and tread us down, and our friends are perplexed and know not what course to take to do us a kindness. The Lord God of hosts is now contending with the valley of vision; the enemies with their battering rams are breaking down the walls, and we are in vain crying to the mountains (to keep off the enemy, or to fall on us and cover us) or looking for help to come to us over the mountains, or appealing, as God does, to the mountains, to hear our controversy (<reference osisRef="Mic.6.1">Mic. vi. 1</reference>) and to judge between us and our injurious neighbours. <div eID="gen15937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15938" type="x-p"/> IV. The great numbers and strength of the enemy, that should invade their country and besiege their city, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6-Isa.22.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Elam (that is, the Persians) come with their quiver full of arrows, and with chariots of fighting men, and horsemen. Kir (that is, the Medes) muster up their arms, unsheath the sword, and uncover the shield, and get every thing ready for battle, every thing ready for the besieging of Jerusalem. Then the choice valleys about Jerusalem, that used to be clothed with flocks and covered over with corn, shall be full of chariots of war, and at the gate of the city <hi type="italic">the horsemen shall set themselves in array,</hi> to cut off all provisions from going in, and to force their way in. What a condition must the city be in that was beset on all sides with such an army!
entries.03c832efc2b037d5eb6e22c8cbb93c9cb4b26522: <div eID="gen15938" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Contempt of Divine Goodness; Contempt of Divine Judgments. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 718.)</title> <div sID="gen15939" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And he discovered the covering of Judah, and thou didst look in that day to the armour of the house of the forest. <hi type="super">9</hi> Ye have seen also the breaches of the city of David, that they are many: and ye gathered together the waters of the lower pool. <hi type="super">10</hi> And ye have numbered the houses of Jerusalem, and the houses have ye broken down to fortify the wall. <hi type="super">11</hi> Ye made also a ditch between the two walls for the water of the old pool: but ye have not looked unto the maker thereof, neither had respect unto him that fashioned it long ago. <hi type="super">12</hi> And in that day did the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts call to weeping, and to mourning, and to baldness, and to girding with sackcloth: <hi type="super">13</hi> And behold joy and gladness, slaying oxen, and killing sheep, eating flesh, and drinking wine: let us eat and drink; for to morrow we shall die. <hi type="super">14</hi> And it was revealed in mine ears by the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till ye die, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen15939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15940" type="x-p"/> What is meant by <hi type="italic">the covering of Judah,</hi> which in the beginning of this paragraph is said to be <hi type="italic">discovered,</hi> is not agreed. The fenced cities of Judah were a covering to the country; but these, being taken by the army of the Assyrians, ceased to be a shelter, so that the whole country lay exposed to be plundered. The weakness of Judah, its nakedness, and inability to keep itself, now appeared more than ever; and thus the covering of Judah was discovered. Its magazines and stores, which had been locked up, were now laid open for the public use. Dr. Lightfoot gives another sense of it, that by this distress into which Judah should be brought God would discover their covering (that is, uncloak their hypocrisy), would show all that was in their heart, as is said of Hezekiah upon another occasion, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.31">2 Chron. xxxii. 31</reference>. Thus, by one means or other, <hi type="italic">the iniquity of Ephraim will be discovered and the sin of Samaria,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.1">Hos. vii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen15940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15941" type="x-p"/> They were now in a great fright, and in this fright they manifested two things much amiss:— <div eID="gen15941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15942" type="x-p"/> I. A great contempt of God's goodness, and his power to help them. They made use of all the means they could think of for their own preservation; and it is not for doing this that they are blamed, but, in doing this, they did not acknowledge God. Observe, <div eID="gen15942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15943" type="x-p"/> 1. How careful they were to improve all advantages that might contribute to their safety. When Sennacherib had made himself master of all the defenced cities of Judah, and Jerusalem was left as a cottage in a vineyard, they thought it was time to look about them. A council was immediately called, a council of war; and it was resolved to stand upon their defence, and not tamely to surrender. Pursuant to this resolve, they took all the prudent measures they could for their own security. We tempt God if, in times of danger, we do not the best we can for ourselves. (1.) They inspected the magazines and stores, to see if they were well stocked with arms and ammunition: <hi type="italic">They looked to the armour of the house of the forest,</hi> which Solomon built in Jerusalem for an armoury (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.17">1 Kings x. 17</reference>), and thence they delivered out what they had occasion for. It is the wisdom of princes, in time of peace, to provide for war, that they may not have arms to seek when they should use them, and perhaps upon a sudden emergency. (2.) They viewed the fortifications, the <hi type="italic">breaches of the city of David;</hi> they walked round the walls, and observed where they had gone to decay for want of seasonable repairs, or were broken by some former attempts made upon them. These breaches were many; the more shame for the house of David that they suffered the city of David to lie neglected. They had probably often seen those breaches; but now they saw them to consider what course to take about them. This good we should get by public distresses, we should be awakened by them to <hi type="italic">repair our breaches,</hi> and amend what is amiss. (3.) They made sure of water for the city, and did what they could to deprive the besiegers of it: <hi type="italic">You gathered together the water of the lower pool,</hi> of which there was probably no great store, and of which therefore they were the more concerned to be good husbands. See what a mercy it is that, as nothing is more necessary to the support of human life than water, so nothing is more cheap and common; but it is bad indeed when that, as here, is a scarce commodity. (4.) They <hi type="italic">numbered the houses of Jerusalem,</hi> that every house might send in its quota of men for the public service, or contribute in money to it, which they raised by a poll, so much a head or so much a house. (5.) Because private property ought to give way to the public safety, those houses that stood in their way, when the wall was to be fortified, were broken down, which, in such a case of necessity, is no more an injury to the owner than blowing up houses in case of fire. (6.) They made a ditch between the outer and inner wall, for the greater security of the city; and they contrived to draw the water of the old pool to it, that they might have plenty of water themselves and might deprive the besiegers of it; for it seems that was the project, lest the Assyrian army <hi type="italic">should come and find much water</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.4">2 Chron. xxxii. 4</reference>) and so should be the better able to prolong the siege. If it be lawful to destroy the forage of a country, much more to divert the streams of its waters, for the straitening and starving of an enemy. <div eID="gen15943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15944" type="x-p"/> 2. How regardless they were of God in all these preparations: <hi type="italic">But you have not looked unto the Maker thereof</hi> (that is, of Jerusalem, the city you are so solicitous for the defence of) and of all the advantages which nature has furnished it with for its defence—the <hi type="italic">mountains round about it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Ps. cxxv. 2</reference>), and the rivers, which were such as the inhabitants might turn which way soever they pleased for their convenience. Note, (1.) It is God that made his Jerusalem, and fashioned it long ago, in his counsels. The Jewish writers, upon this place, say, There were seven things which God made before the world (meaning which he had in his eye when he made the world): <hi type="italic">the garden of Eden, the law, the just ones, Israel, the throne of glory, Jerusalem, and Messiah the Prince.</hi> The gospel church has God for its Maker. (2.) Whatever service we do, or endeavour to do, at any time to God's Jerusalem, must be done with an eye to him as the Maker of it; and he takes it ill if it be done otherwise. It is here charged upon them that they did not look to God. [1.] They did not design his glory in what they did. They fortified Jerusalem because it was a rich city and their own houses were in it, not because it was the holy city and God's house was in it. In all our cares for the defence of the church we must look more at God's interest in it than at our own. [2.] They did not depend upon him for a blessing upon their endeavours, saw no need of it, and therefore sought not to him for it, but thought their own powers and policies sufficient for them. Of Hezekiah himself it is said that <hi type="italic">he trusted in God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.5">2 Kings xviii. 5</reference>), and particularly upon this occasion (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.8">2 Chron. xxxii. 8</reference>); but there were those about him, it seems, who were great statesmen and soldiers, but had little religion in them. [3.] They did not give him thanks for the advantages they had, in fortifying their city, from <hi type="italic">the waters of the old pool,</hi> which were fashioned long ago, as Kishon is called <hi type="italic">an ancient river,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.21">Judg. v. 21</reference>. Whatever in nature is at any time serviceable to us, we must therein acknowledge the goodness of the God of nature, who, when he fashioned it long ago, fitted it to be so, and <hi type="italic">according to whose ordinance it continues to this day.</hi> Every creature is that to us which God makes it to be; and therefore, whatever use it is of to us, we must <hi type="italic">look at him that fashioned it,</hi> bless him for it, and use it for him. <div eID="gen15944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15945" type="x-p"/> II. A great contempt of God's wrath and justice in contending with them, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.14">v. 12-14</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen15945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15946" type="x-p"/> 1. What was God's design in bringing this calamity upon them: it was to humble them, bring them to repentance, and make them serious. In that day of trouble, and treading down, and perplexity, the Lord did thereby <hi type="italic">call to weeping and mourning,</hi> and all the expressions of sorrow, even <hi type="italic">to baldness and girding with sackcloth;</hi> and all this to lament their sins (by which they had brought those judgments upon their land), to enforce their prayers (by which they might hope to avert the judgments that were breaking in), and to dispose themselves to a reformation of their lives by a holy seriousness and a tenderness of heart under the word of God. To this God called them by his prophet's explaining his providences, and by his providences awakening them to regard what his prophets said. Note, When God threatens us with his judgments he expects and requires that we humble ourselves under his mighty hand, that we tremble when the lion roars, and in a day of adversity consider. <div eID="gen15946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15947" type="x-p"/> 2. How contrary they walked to this design of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, joy and gladness,</hi> mirth and feasting, all the gaiety and all the jollity imaginable. They were as secure and cheerful as they used to be, as if they had had no enemy in their borders or were in no danger of falling into his hands. When they had taken the necessary precautions for their security, then they set all deaths and dangers at defiance, and resolved to be merry, let come on them what would. Those that should have been among the mourners were among the <hi type="italic">wine-bibbers, the riotous eaters of flesh;</hi> and observe what they said, <hi type="italic">Let us eat and drink, for to-morrow we shall die.</hi> This may refer either to the particular danger they were now in, and the fair warning which the prophet gave them of it, or to the general shortness and uncertainty of human life, and the nearness of death at all times. This was the language of the profane scoffers who <hi type="italic">mocked the messengers of the Lord and misused his prophets.</hi> (1.) They made a jest of dying. "The prophet tells us we must die shortly, perhaps to-morrow, and therefore we should mourn and repent to-day; no, rather <hi type="italic">let us eat and drink,</hi> that we may be fattened for the slaughter, and may be in good heart to meet our doom; if we must have a short life, let it be a merry one." (2.) They ridiculed the doctrine of a future state on the other side death; for, if there were no such state, the apostle grants there would be something of reason in what they said, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1 Cor. xv. 32</reference>. If, when we die, there were an end of us, it were good to make ourselves as easy and merry as we could while we live; but, if <hi type="italic">for all these things God shall bring us into judgment,</hi> it is at our peril if we walk <hi type="italic">in the way of our heart and the sight of our eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>. Note, A practical disbelief of another life after this is at the bottom of the carnal security and brutish sensuality which are the sin, and shame, and ruin of so great a part of mankind, as of the old world, who were <hi type="italic">eating and drinking till the flood came.</hi> <div eID="gen15947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15948" type="x-p"/> 3. How much God was displeased at it. He signified his resentment of it to the prophet, <hi type="italic">revealed it in his ears,</hi> to be by him proclaimed upon the house-top: <hi type="italic">Surely this iniquity shall not be purged from you till you die,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.14">v. 14</reference>. It shall never be expiated with sacrifice and offering, any more than the iniquity of the house of Eli, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.14">1 Sam. iii. 14</reference>. It is a sin against the remedy, a baffling of the utmost means of conviction and rendering them ineffectual; and therefore it is not likely they should ever repent of it or have it pardoned. The Chaldee reads it, <hi type="italic">It shall not be forgiven you till you die the second death.</hi> Those that walk contrary to them; with the froward he will show himself froward.
entries.791bd0dc61d053d3365fe19e9845e35ed6f47107: <div eID="gen15948" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Downfall of Shebna; The Advancement of Eliakim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 714.)</title> <div sID="gen15949" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> of hosts, Go, get thee unto this treasurer, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Shebna, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> over the house, <hi type="italic">and say,</hi> <hi type="super">16</hi> What hast thou here? and whom hast thou here, that thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre here, <hi type="italic">as</hi> he that heweth him out a sepulchre on high, <hi type="italic">and</hi> that graveth a habitation for himself in a rock? <hi type="super">17</hi> Behold, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will carry thee away with a mighty captivity, and will surely cover thee. <hi type="super">18</hi> He will surely violently turn and toss thee <hi type="italic">like</hi> a ball into a large country: there shalt thou die, and there the chariots of thy glory <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> the shame of thy lord's house. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I will drive thee from thy station, and from thy state shall he pull thee down. <hi type="super">20</hi> And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah: <hi type="super">21</hi> And I will clothe him with thy robe, and strengthen him with thy girdle, and I will commit thy government into his hand: and he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and to the house of Judah. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. <hi type="super">23</hi> And I will fasten him <hi type="italic">as</hi> a nail in a sure place; and he shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father's house, the offspring and the issue, all vessels of small quantity, from the vessels of cups, even to all the vessels of flagons. <hi type="super">25</hi> In that day, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, shall the nail that is fastened in the sure place be removed, and be cut down, and fall; and the burden that <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon it shall be cut off: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen15949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15950" type="x-p"/> We have here a prophecy concerning the displacing of Shebna, a great officer at court, and the preferring of Eliakim to the post of honour and trust that he was in. Such changes are common in the courts of princes; it is therefore strange that so much notice should be taken of it by the prophet here; but by the accomplishment of what was foretold concerning these particular persons God designed to confirm his word in the mouth of Isaiah concerning other and greater events; and it is likewise to show that, as God has burdens in store for those nations and kingdoms abroad that are open enemies to his church and people, so he has for those particular persons at home that are false friends to them and betray them. It is likewise a confirmation in general of the hand of divine Providence in all events of this kind, which to us seem contingent and to depend upon the wills and fancies of princes. <hi type="italic">Promotion comes not from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south; but God is the Judge,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.6-Ps.25.7">Ps. xxv. 6, 7</reference>. It is probable that this prophecy was delivered at the same time with that in the former part of the chapter, and began to be fulfilled before Sennacherib's invasion; for now Shebna was <hi type="italic">over the house,</hi> but then Eliakim was (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.3">ch. xxxvi. 3</reference>); and Shebna, coming down gradually, was only scribe. Here is, <div eID="gen15950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15951" type="x-p"/> I. The prophecy of Shebna's disgrace. He is called <hi type="italic">this treasurer,</hi> being entrusted with the management of the revenue; and he is likewise said to be <hi type="italic">over the house,</hi> for such was his boundless ambition and covetousness that less than two places, and those two of the greatest importance at court, would not satisfy him. It is common for self-seeking men thus to grasp at more than they can manage, and so the business of their places is neglected, while the pomp and profit of them wholly engage the mind. It does not appear what were the particular instances of Shebna's mal-administration, for which Isaiah is here sent to prophesy against him; but the Jews say, "He kept up a traitorous correspondence with the king of Assyria, and was in treaty with him to deliver the city into his hands." However this was, it should seem that he was a foreigner (for we never read of the name of his father) and that he was an enemy to the true interests of Judah and Jerusalem: it is probable that he was first preferred by Ahaz. Hezekiah was himself an excellent prince; but the best masters cannot always be sure of good servants. We have need to pray for princes, that they may be wise and happy in the choice of those they trust. These were times of reformation, yet Shebna, a bad man, complied so far as to keep his places at court; and it is probable that many others did like him, for which reason Sennacherib is said to have been <hi type="italic">sent against a hypocritical nation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">ch. x. 6</reference>. In this message to Shebna we have, <div eID="gen15951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15952" type="x-p"/> 1. A reproof of his pride, vanity, and security (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">What hast thou here, and whom hast thou here?</hi> What a mighty noise and bustle dost thou make! What estate has thou here, that thou was born to? <hi type="italic">Whom hast thou here,</hi> what relations, that thou art allied to? Art thou not of mean and obscure original, <hi type="italic">filius populi—a mere plebeian,</hi> that comest we know not whence? What is the meaning of this then, that thou hast built thyself a fine house, <hi type="italic">hast graved thyself a habitation?</hi>" So very nice and curious was it that it seemed rather to be the work of an engraver than of a mason or carpenter; and it seemed engraven in a rock, so firmly was it founded and so impregnable was it. "Nay, <hi type="italic">thou hast hewed thee out a sepulchre,</hi>" as if he designed that his pomp should survive his funeral. Though Jerusalem was not <hi type="italic">the place of his father's sepulchres</hi> (as Nehemiah called it with a great deal of tenderness, <reference osisRef="Neh.2.3">Neh. ii. 3</reference>), he designed it should be the place of his own, and therefore set up a monument for himself in his life-time, set it up on high. Those that make stately monuments for their pride forget that, how beautiful soever they appear outwardly, within <hi type="italic">they are full of dead men's bones.</hi> But it is a pity that the grave-stone should forget the grave. <div eID="gen15952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15953" type="x-p"/> 2. A prophecy of his fall and the sullying of his glory. (1.) That he should not quickly be displaced and degraded (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will drive thee from thy station.</hi> High places are slippery places; and those are justly deprived of their honour that are proud of it and puffed up with it, and deprived of their power that do hurt with it. God will do it, who shows himself to be God by <hi type="italic">looking upon proud men and abasing them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.25">v. 25</reference> refers. "The nail that is <hi type="italic">now fastened in the sure place</hi> (that is, Shebna, who thinks himself immovably fixed in his office) <hi type="italic">shall be removed, and cut down, and fall.</hi>" Those are mistaken who think any place in this world a sure place, or themselves as nails fastened in it; for there is nothing here but uncertainty. When the nail falls the burden that was upon it is cut off; when Shebna was disgraced all that had a dependence upon him fell into contempt too. Those that are in high places will have many hanging upon them as favourites whom they are proud of and trust to; but they are burdens upon them, and perhaps with their weight break the nail, and both fall together, and by deceiving ruin one another—the common fate of great men and their flatterers, who expect more from each other than either performs. (2.) That after a while he should not only be driven from his station, but driven from his country: <hi type="italic">The Lord will carry thee away with the captivity of a mighty man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.17-Isa.22.18">v. 17, 18</reference>. Some think the Assyrians seized him, and took him away, because he had promised to assist them and did not, but appeared against them: or perhaps Hezekiah, finding out his treachery, banished him, and forbade him ever to return; or he himself, finding that he had become obnoxious to the people, withdrew into some other country, and there spent the rest of his days in meanness and obscurity. Grotius thinks he was stricken with a leprosy, which was a disease commonly supposed to come from the immediate hand of God's displeasure, particularly for the punishment of the proud, as in the case of Miriam and Uzziah; and by reason of this disease he was <hi type="italic">tossed like a ball</hi> out of Jerusalem. Those who, when they are in power, turn and toss others, will be justly turned and tossed themselves when their day shall come to fall. Many who have thought themselves fastened like a nail may come to be tossed like a ball; for here have we <hi type="italic">no continuing city.</hi> Shebna thought his place too strait for him, he had no room to thrive; God will therefore send him <hi type="italic">into a large country,</hi> where he shall have room to wander, but never find the way back again; for <hi type="italic">there he shall die,</hi> and lay his bones there, and not in the sepulchre he had hewn out for himself. And <hi type="italic">there the chariots</hi> which had been the chariots of his glory, in which he had rattled about the streets of Jerusalem, and which he took into banishment with him, should but serve to upbraid him with his former grandeur, <hi type="italic">to the shame of his lord's house,</hi> of the court of Ahaz, who had advanced him. <div eID="gen15953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15954" type="x-p"/> II. The prophecy of Eliakim's advancement, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.20">v. 20</reference>, &c. He is God's servant, has approved himself faithfully so in other employments, and therefore God will call him to this high station. Those that are diligent in doing the duty of a low sphere stand fairest for preferment in God's books. Eliakim does not undermine Shebna, nor make an interest against him, nor does he intrude into his office; but God calls him to it: and what God calls us to we may expect he will own us in. It is here foretold, 1. That Eliakim should be put into Shebna's place of lord-chamberlain of the household, lord-treasurer, and prime-minister of state. The prophet must tell Shebna this, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">v. 21</reference>. "He shall have <hi type="italic">thy robe,</hi> the badge of honour, and <hi type="italic">thy girdle,</hi> the badge of power; for he shall have <hi type="italic">thy government.</hi>" To hear of it would be a great mortification to Shebna, much more to see it. Great men, especially if proud men, cannot endure their successors. God undertakes the doing of it, not only because he would put it into the heart of Hezekiah to do it, and his hand must be acknowledged guiding the hearts of princes in placing and displacing men (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.1">Prov. xxi. 1</reference>), but because the powers that are, subordinate as well as supreme, are ordained of God. It is God that clothes princes with their robes, and therefore we must submit ourselves to them for the Lord's sake and with an eye to him, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13">1 Pet. ii. 13</reference>. And, since it is he that <hi type="italic">commits the government into their hand,</hi> they must administer it according to his will, for his glory; they must judge for him by whom they judge and <hi type="italic">decree justice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.8.15">Prov. viii. 15</reference>. And they may depend upon him to furnish them for what he calls them to, according to this promise: <hi type="italic">I will clothe him;</hi> and then it follows, <hi type="italic">I will strengthen him.</hi> Those that are called to places of trust and power should seek unto God for grace to enable them to do the duty of their places; for that ought to be their chief care. Eliakim's advancement is further described by the laying of the <hi type="italic">key of the house of David upon his shoulders,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">v. 22</reference>. Probably he carried a golden key upon his shoulder as a badge of his office, or had one embroidered upon his cloak or robe, to which this alludes. Being over the house, and having the key delivered to him, as the seals are to the lord-keeper, <hi type="italic">he shall open and none shall shut, shut and none shall open.</hi> He had access to <hi type="italic">the house of the precious things, the silver, and the gold, and the spices;</hi> and to the <hi type="italic">house of the armour</hi> and the <hi type="italic">treasures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.2">ch. xxxix. 2</reference>), and disposed of the stores there as he thought fit for the public service. He put whom he pleased into the inferior offices and turned out whom he pleased. Our Lord Jesus describes his own power as Mediator by an allusion to this (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Rev. iii. 7</reference>), that <hi type="italic">he has the key of David,</hi> wherewith he <hi type="italic">opens and no man shuts,</hi> he <hi type="italic">shuts and no man opens.</hi> His power in the kingdom of heaven, and in the ordering of all the affairs of that kingdom, is absolute, irresistible, and uncontrollable. 2. That he should be fixed and confirmed in that office. He shall have it for life, and not <hi type="italic">durante bene placito—during pleasure</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place,</hi> not to be removed or cut down. Thus lasting shall the honour be that comes from God to all those who use it for him. Our Lord Jesus is <hi type="italic">as a nail in a sure place:</hi> his kingdom cannot be shaken, and he himself is still the same. 3. That he should be a great blessing in his office; and it is this that crowns the favours here conferred upon him. God <hi type="italic">makes his name great,</hi> for he shall be a blessing, <reference osisRef="Gen.12.2">Gen. xii. 2</reference>. (1.) He shall be a blessing to his country (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.</hi> he shall take care not only of the affairs of the king's household, but of all the public interests in Jerusalem and Judah. Note, Rulers should be fathers to those that are under their government, to teach them with wisdom, rule them with love, and correct what is amiss with tenderness, to protect them and provide for them, and be solicitous about them as a man is for his own children and family. It is happy with a people when the court, the city, and the country, have no separate interests, but all centre in the same, so that the courtiers are true patriots, and whom the court blesses the country has reason to bless too; and when those who are fathers to Jerusalem, the royal city, are no less so to the house of Judah. (2.) He shall be a blessing to his family (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.23-Isa.22.24">v. 23, 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall be for a glorious throne to his father's house.</hi> The consummate wisdom and virtue which recommended him to this great trust made him the honour of his family, which probably was very considerable before, but now became much more so. Children should aim to be a credit to their parents and relations. The honour men reflect upon their families by their piety and usefulness is more to be valued than that which they derive from their families by their names and titles. Eliakim being preferred, <hi type="italic">all the glory of his father's house</hi> was hung upon him; they all made their court to him, and his brethren's sheaves bowed to his. Observe, The glory of this world gives a man no intrinsic worth or excellency; it is but hung upon him as an appurtenance, and it will soon drop from him. Eliakim was compared to <hi type="italic">a nail in a sure place,</hi> in pursuance of which comparison all the relations of his family (which, it is likely, were numerous, and that was the glory of it) are said to have a dependence upon him, as in a house the vessels that have handles to them are hung up upon nails and pins. It intimates likewise that he shall generously take care of them all, and bear the weight of that care: <hi type="italic">All the vessels,</hi> not only <hi type="italic">the flagons,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the cups, the vessels of small quantity,</hi> the meanest that belong to his family, shall be provided for by him. See what a burden those bring upon themselves that undertake great trusts; they little think how many and how much will hand upon them if they resolve to be faithful in the discharge of their trust. Our Lord Jesus, having the key of the house of David, is as a <hi type="italic">nail in a sure place,</hi> and all <hi type="italic">the glory of his father's house hangs</hi> upon him, is derived from him, and depends upon him; even the meanest that belong to his church are welcome to him, and he is able to bear the stress of them all. That soul cannot perish, nor that concern fall to the ground, though ever so weighty, that is by faith hung upon Christ.  <chapter eID="Isa.22"/> <div eID="gen15954" type="x-p"/>

entries.920f899b2e753ef33564c4cea35b97578e79b873: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8693"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.22.1-Isa.22.14">Is 22:1-14</reference>. Prophecy as to an Attack on Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen14361" type="x-p"/> That by Sennacherib, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.11">Is 22:8-11</reference>, the preparations for defense and securing of water exactly answer to those in <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.4">2Ch 32:4</reference>, 5, 30. "Shebna," too (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.15">Is 22:15</reference>), was scribe at this time (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.3">Is 36:3</reference>) [Maurer]. The language of <reference osisRef="Isa.22.12-Isa.22.14">Is 22:12-14</reference>, as to the infidelity and consequent utter ruin of the Jews, seems rather to foreshadow the destruction by Nebuchadnezzar in Zedekiah's reign, and cannot be restricted to Hezekiah's time [Lowth].<div eID="gen14361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8693"/><hi type="bold">1. of ... valley of vision--</hi>rather, "respecting the valley of visions"; namely, Jerusalem, the seat of divine revelations and visions, "the nursery of prophets" [Jerome], (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Is 2:3</reference>; 29:1; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.4">Eze 23:4</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.33">Lu 13:33</reference>). It lay in a "valley" surrounded by hills higher than Zion and Moriah (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.2">Psa 125:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jr 21:13</reference>).<div eID="gen14362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thee--</hi>the people of Jerusalem personified.<div eID="gen14363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">housetops--</hi>Panic-struck, they went up on the flat balustraded roofs to look forth and see whether the enemy was near, and partly to defend themselves from the roofs (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.51">Jud 9:51</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen14364" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f35545f910fa658f86f216a97f25ef5d91b73f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8694"/><div sID="gen14365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8694"/><hi type="bold">2. art--</hi>rather, "wert"; for it could not now be said to be "a joyous city" (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Is 32:13</reference>). The cause of their joy (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Is 22:13</reference>) may have been because Sennacherib had accepted Hezekiah's offer to renew the payment of tribute, and they were glad to have peace on any terms, however humiliating (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2Ki 18:14-16</reference>), or on account of the alliance with Egypt. If the reference be to Zedekiah's time, the joy and feasting are not inapplicable, for this recklessness was a general characteristic of the unbelieving Jews (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">Is 56:12</reference>).<div eID="gen14365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not slain with the sword--</hi>but with the famine and pestilence about to be caused by the coming siege (<reference osisRef="Lam.4.9">La 4:9</reference>). Maurer refers this to the plague by which he thinks Sennacherib's army was destroyed, and Hezekiah was made sick (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.1">38:1</reference>). But there is no authority for supposing that the Jews in the city suffered such extremities of plague at this time, when God destroyed their foes. Barnes refers it to those slain in flight, not in open honorable "battle"; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.3">Is 22:3</reference> favors this. <div eID="gen14366" type="x-p"/>
entries.a52c715854e2be78d45016fd8e05be65a76cbda8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8695"/><div sID="gen14367" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8695"/><hi type="bold">3. rulers--</hi>rather, "generals" (<reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.11.6">Jud 11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.11.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen14367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14368" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bound--</hi>rather, "are taken."<div eID="gen14368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by the archers--</hi>literally, "by the bow"; so <reference osisRef="Isa.21.17">Is 21:17</reference>. Bowmen were the light troops, whose province it was to skirmish in front and (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.22">2Ki 6:22</reference>) pursue fugitives (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.5">2Ki 25:5</reference>); this verse applies better to the attack of Nebuchadnezzar than that of Sennacherib.<div eID="gen14369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14370" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... in thee--</hi>all found in the city (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.15">Is 13:15</reference>), not merely the "rulers" or generals.<div eID="gen14370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fled from far--</hi>those who had fled from distant parts to Jerusalem as a place of safety; rather, fled afar. <div eID="gen14371" type="x-p"/>
entries.c910c17995841ce235cf87e8ad0db9dcb8704d16: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8696"/><div sID="gen14372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8696"/><hi type="bold">4. Look ... from me--</hi>Deep grief seeks to be alone; while others feast joyously, Isaiah mourns in prospect of the disaster coming on Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Mic.1.8">Mi 1:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen14372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14373" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughter, &c.--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.8">Is 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">La 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen14373" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4a86d4124bb00038443feea5d895a60eae43f9f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8697"/><div sID="gen14374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8697"/><hi type="bold">5. trouble ... by the Lord--</hi>that is, sent by or from the Lord (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.19.15">Is 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.22-Luke.21.24">Lu 21:22-24</reference>).<div eID="gen14374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">valley of vision--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.1">Is 22:1</reference>). Some think a valley near Ophel is meant as about to be the scene of devastation (compare see on <reference osisRef="Isa.32.13">Is 32:13</reference>,<reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen14375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">breaking ... walls--</hi>that is, "a day of breaking the walls" of the city.<div eID="gen14376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">crying to the mountains--</hi>the mournful cry of the townsmen "reaches" to (Maurer translates, towards) the mountains, and is echoed back by them. Josephus describes in the very same language the scene at the assault of Jerusalem under Titus. To this the prophecy, probably, refers ultimately. If, as some think, the "cry" is that of those escaping to the mountains, compare <reference osisRef="Matt.13.14">Mt 13:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">24:16</reference>, with this. <div eID="gen14377" type="x-p"/>
entries.7291dea6c84fb2c9e5b6768a5abf391fc4529ccc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8698"/><div sID="gen14378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8698"/><hi type="bold">6. Elam--</hi>the country stretching east from the Lower Tigris, answering to what was afterwards called Persia (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Is 21:2</reference>). Later, Elam was a province of Persia (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.9">Ezr 4:9</reference>). In Sennacherib's time, Elam was subject to Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.11">2Ki 18:11</reference>), and so furnished a contingent to its invading armies. Famed for the bow (<reference osisRef="Isa.13.18">Is 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.35">Jr 49:35</reference>), in which the Ethiopians alone excelled them.<div eID="gen14378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with chariots of men and horsemen--</hi>that is, they used the bow both in chariots and on horseback. "Chariots of men," that is, chariots in which men are borne, war chariots (compare see on <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>).<div eID="gen14379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kir--</hi>another people subject to Assyria (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Ki 16:9</reference>); the region about the river Kur, between the Caspian and Black Seas.<div eID="gen14380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14381" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">uncovered--</hi>took off for the battle the leather covering of the shield, intended to protect the embossed figures on it from dust or injury during the march. "The quiver" and "the shield" express two classes--light and heavy armed troops. <div eID="gen14381" type="x-p"/>
entries.89920e9e72a1c47627f08584e0ce8f60f9331930: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8699"/><div sID="gen14382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8699"/><hi type="bold">7. valleys--</hi>east, north, and south of Jerusalem: Hinnom on the south side was the richest valley.<div eID="gen14382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in array at the gate--</hi>Rab-shakeh stood at the upper pool close to the city (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.11-Isa.36.13">Is 36:11-13</reference>). <div eID="gen14383" type="x-p"/>
entries.63a1e9bd10d9cefffa392b1b54b6ee46541692be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8700"/><div sID="gen14384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8700"/><hi type="bold">8. he discovered the covering--</hi>rather, "the veil of Judah shall be taken off" [Horsley]: figuratively for, exposing to shame as a captive (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Is 47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.5">Na 3:5</reference>). Sennacherib dismantled all "the defensed cities of Judah" (<reference osisRef="Isa.36.1">Is 36:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou didst look--</hi>rather, "thou shalt look."<div eID="gen14385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14386" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house of ... forest--</hi>The house of armory built of cedar from the forest of Lebanon by Solomon, on a slope of Zion called Ophel (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.2">1Ki 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.17">10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Ne 3:19</reference>). Isaiah says (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.13">Is 22:8-13</reference>) his countrymen will look to their own strength to defend themselves, while others of them will drown their sorrows as to their country in feasting, but none will look to Jehovah. <div eID="gen14386" type="x-p"/>
entries.f077fa89c5395415f92b3cd1c2fcdcec5a8412ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8701"/><div sID="gen14387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8701"/><hi type="bold">9. Ye have seen--</hi>rather, "Ye shall see."<div eID="gen14387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14388" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">city of David--</hi>the upper city, on Zion, the south side of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7">2Sa 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.1">1Ki 8:1</reference>); surrounded by a wall of its own; but even in it there shall be "breaches." Hezekiah's preparations for defense accord with this (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14389" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye gathered--</hi>rather, "ye shall gather."<div eID="gen14389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lower pool--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Is 22:11</reference>). Ye shall bring together into the city by subterranean passages cut in the rock of Zion, the fountain from which the lower pool (only mentioned here) is supplied. See on <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Is 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.20">2Ki 20:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3-2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:3-5</reference>, represent Hezekiah as having stopped the fountains to prevent the Assyrians getting water. But this is consistent with the passage here. The superfluous waters of the lower pool usually flowed into Hinnom valley, and so through that of Jehoshaphat to the brook Kedron. Hezekiah built a wall round it, stopped the outflowing of its waters to debar the foe from the use of them, and turned them into the city. <div eID="gen14390" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bb9180145a20d4aa38315980a8d7a7cc777c192: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8702"/><div sID="gen14391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8702"/><hi type="bold">10. numbered--</hi>rather, "ye shall number," namely, in order to see which of them may be pulled down with the least loss to the city, and with most advantage for the repair of the walls and rearing of towers (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Ch 32:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have ye broken down--</hi>rather, "ye shall break down." <div eID="gen14392" type="x-p"/>
entries.862f2200c64af850b285c68f9237d6e6613d50c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8703"/><div sID="gen14393" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8703"/><hi type="bold">11. Ye made ... a ditch--</hi>rather, "Ye shall make a reservoir" for receiving the water. Hezekiah surrounded Siloah, from which the old (or king's, or upper) pool took its rise, with a wall joined to the wall of Zion on both sides; between these two walls he made a new pool, into which he directed the waters of the former, thus cutting off the foe from his supply of water also. The opening from which the upper pool received its water was nearer Zion than the other from which the lower pool took its rise, so that the water which flowed from the former could easily be shut in by a wall, whereas that which flowed from the latter could only be brought in by subterranean conduits (compare see on <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">Is 22:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Is 7:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.20">2Ki 20:20</reference>; 2Ch 32:3-5, 30; Ecclesiasticus 48:17). Both were southwest of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen14393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have not looked ... neither had respect--</hi>answering by contrast to "Thou didst look to the armor, ye have seen ('had respect', or 'regard to') the breaches" (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.8">Is 22:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen14394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14395" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maker thereof--</hi>God, by whose command and aid these defenses were made, and who gave this fountain "long ago." G. V. Smith translates, "Him who doeth it," that is, has brought this danger on you--"Him who hath prepared it from afar," that is, planned it even from a distant time. <div eID="gen14395" type="x-p"/>
entries.67e5e4d786816358b89b6a662f066aa90d93a675: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8704"/><div sID="gen14396" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8704"/><hi type="bold">12. did the Lord God call--</hi>Usually the priests gave the summons to national mourning (<reference osisRef="Joel.1.14">Joe 1:14</reference>); now Jehovah Himself shall give it; the "call" shall consist in the presence of a terrible foe. Translate, "shall call."<div eID="gen14396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">baldness--</hi>emblem of grief (<reference osisRef="Job.1.20">Job 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.1.16">Mi 1:16</reference>). <div eID="gen14397" type="x-p"/>
entries.adf1777d953cc423a5b7c3faf953ff7fc1644bbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8705"/><div sID="gen14398" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8705"/>13. Notwithstanding Jehovah's "call to mourning" (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.12">Is 22:12</reference>), many shall make the desperate state of affairs a reason for reckless revelry (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>, 12, 14; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">Jr 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.32">1Co 15:32</reference>).<div eID="gen14398" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.22.15-Isa.22.25">Is 22:15-25</reference>. Prophecy That Shebna Should Be Deposed from Being Prefect of the Palace, and Eliakim Promoted to the Office.</title> <div sID="gen14399" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.36.3">Is 36:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.2">37:2</reference>, we find Shebna "a scribe," and no longer prefect of the palace ("over the household"), and Eliakim in that office, as is here foretold. Shebna is singled out as the subject of prophecy (the only instance of an individual being so in Isaiah), as being one of the irreligious faction that set at naught the prophet's warnings (Is 28:1-33:24); perhaps it was he who advised the temporary ignominious submission of Hezekiah to Sennacherib. <div eID="gen14399" type="x-p"/>
entries.b38c1a6d1e0aa4dc3f07c7e8a8ded835901adbbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8706"/><div sID="gen14400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8706"/><hi type="bold">15. Go, get thee unto--</hi>rather, "Go in to" (that is, into the house to).<div eID="gen14400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">treasurer--</hi>"him who dwells in the tabernacle" [Jerome]; namely, in a room of the temple set apart for the treasurer. Rather, "the king's friend," or "principal officer of the court" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.5">1Ki 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.3">18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.33">1Ch 27:33</reference>, "the king's counsellor") [Maurer]. "This" is prefixed contemptuously (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1">Ex 32:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14402" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto Shebna--</hi>The Hebrew for "unto" indicates an accosting of Shebna with an unwelcome message. <div eID="gen14402" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c4a29ef24ee1f1f78c52b5b12724b0d8895895c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8707"/><div sID="gen14403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8707"/><hi type="bold">16. What ... whom--</hi>The prophet accosts Shebna at the very place where he was building a grand sepulcher for himself and his family (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.18">Is 14:18</reference>; Ge 23:1-20; 49:29; 50:13). "What (business) hast thou here, and whom hast thou (of thy family, who is likely to be buried) here, that thou buildest," &c., seeing that thou art soon to be deposed from office and carried into captivity? [Maurer].<div eID="gen14403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on high--</hi>Sepulchres were made in the highest rocks (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.33">2Ch 32:33</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen14404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14405" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">habitation for himself--</hi>compare "his own house" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.18">Is 14:18</reference>). <div eID="gen14405" type="x-p"/>
entries.955abaa40ecaef70ffad35328d651b7346141abe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8708"/><div sID="gen14406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8708"/><hi type="bold">17. carry ... away with ... captivity--</hi>rather, "will cast thee away with a mighty throw" [Maurer]. "Mighty," literally, "of a man" (so <reference osisRef="Job.38.3">Job 38:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14407" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">surely cover--</hi>namely, with shame, where thou art rearing a monument to perpetuate thy fame [Vitringa]. "Rolling will roll thee," that is, will continually roll thee on, as a ball to be tossed away [Maurer]. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Is 22:18</reference>. <div eID="gen14407" type="x-p"/>
entries.c616226f8f73c01361b3281ebe40379ec33ffce6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8709"/><div sID="gen14408" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8709"/><hi type="bold">18. violently turn and toss--</hi>literally, "whirling He will whirl thee," that is, He will, without intermission, whirl thee [Maurer]. "He will whirl thee round and round, and (then) cast thee away," as a stone in a sling is first whirled round repeatedly, before the string is let go [Lowth].<div eID="gen14408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14409" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">large country--</hi>perhaps Assyria.<div eID="gen14409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chariots ... shall be the shame of thy lord's house--</hi>rather, "thy splendid chariots shall be there, O thou disgrace of thy lord's house" [Noyes]; "chariots of thy glory" mean "thy magnificent chariots." It is not meant that he would have these in a distant land, as he had in Jerusalem, but that he would be borne thither in ignominy instead of in his magnificent chariots. The Jews say that he was tied to the tails of horses by the enemy, to whom he had designed to betray Jerusalem, as they thought he was mocking them; and so he died. <div eID="gen14410" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a45a6e7e534d505d145c80b2bbdc4c4f4fa38f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8710"/><div sID="gen14411" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8710"/><hi type="bold">19. state--</hi>office.<div eID="gen14411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14412" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God. A similar change of persons occurs in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Is 34:16</reference>. <div eID="gen14412" type="x-p"/>
entries.c963a60a69d970f2952c07185f80d95be7772399: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8711"/><div sID="gen14413" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8711"/><hi type="bold">20. son of Hilkiah--</hi>supposed by Kimchi to be the same as Azariah, son of Hilkiah, who perhaps had two names, and who was "over the household" in Hezekiah's time (<reference osisRef="1Chr.6.13">1Ch 6:13</reference>). <div eID="gen14413" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc41b529bb7e8aab808ba29bc34460de471d30a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8712"/><div sID="gen14414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8712"/><hi type="bold">21. thy robe--</hi>of office.<div eID="gen14414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14415" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">girdle--</hi>in which the purse was carried, and to it was attached the sword; often adorned with gold and jewels.<div eID="gen14415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14416" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">father--</hi>that is, a counsellor and friend. <div eID="gen14416" type="x-p"/>
entries.426d8f54f561b97d0616dbd7e355c2a732d25814: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8713"/><div sID="gen14417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8713"/><hi type="bold">22. key--</hi>emblem of his office over the house; to "open" or "shut"; access rested with him.<div eID="gen14417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon ... shoulder--</hi>So keys are carried sometimes in the East, hanging from the kerchief on the shoulder. But the phrase is rather figurative for sustaining the government on one's shoulders. Eliakim, as his name implies, is here plainly a type of the God-man Christ, the son of "David," of whom Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) uses the same language as the former clause of this verse. In <reference osisRef="Rev.3.7">Re 3:7</reference>, the same language as the latter clause is found (compare <reference osisRef="Job.12.14">Job 12:14</reference>). <div eID="gen14418" type="x-p"/>
entries.463a33fac80bb754607bce83356a4b49b44fd6d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8714"/><div sID="gen14419" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8714"/><hi type="bold">23. nail ... sure place--</hi>Large nails or pegs stood in ancient houses on which were suspended the ornaments of the family. The sense is: all that is valuable to the nation shall rest securely on him. In <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.8">Ezr 9:8</reference> "nail" is used of the large spike driven into the ground to fasten the cords of the tent to.<div eID="gen14419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14420" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne--</hi>resting-place to his family, as applied to Eliakim; but "throne," in the strict sense, as applied to Messiah, the antitype (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.32">Lu 1:32</reference>, 33). <div eID="gen14420" type="x-p"/>
entries.844b12b52456827e2c1b833721f08754d3368357: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8715"/><div sID="gen14421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8715"/>24. Same image as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.23">Is 22:23</reference>. It was customary to "hang" the valuables of a house on nails (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.16">1Ki 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.21">17, 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.4">So 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen14421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offspring and the issue--</hi>rather, "the offshoots of the family, high and low" [Vitringa]. Eliakim would reflect honor even on the latter.<div eID="gen14422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessels of cups--</hi>of small capacity: answering to the low and humble offshoots.<div eID="gen14423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vessels of flagons--</hi>larger vessels: answering to the high offshoots. <div eID="gen14424" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7a27681d86e447957f71156ea92d40933e20e41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8716"/><div sID="gen14425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8716"/><hi type="bold">25. nail ... fastened--</hi>Shebna, who was supposed to be firmly fixed in his post.<div eID="gen14425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14426" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burden ... upon it--</hi>All that were dependent on Shebna, all his emoluments and rank will fail, as when a peg is suddenly "cut down," the ornaments on it fall with it. Sin reaches in its effects even to the family of the guilty (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.22"/>

entries.9e939a1b88c4e80988c28b0c2196f935199acbdc: <div eID="gen27360" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27362" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27361" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> Prophecy concerning Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.1-Isa.22.14">Isa 22:1-14</reference>. Sentence against Shebna, who was over the household, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.15-Isa.22.19">Isa 22:15-19</reference>. Prophecy concerning Eliakim, the son of Hilkiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.20">Isa 22:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.21">Isa 22:21</reference>. From Eliakim, Isaiah, (agreeably to the mode universally adopted in the prophetical writings, of making the things then present, or which were shortly to be accomplished, types or representations of things to be fulfilled upon a larger scale in distant futurity), makes a transition to the Messiah, of whom Eliakim was a type, to whom the words will best apply, and to whom some passages in the prophecy must be solely restrained, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.20-Isa.22.24">Isa 22:20-24</reference>. The sentence against Shebna again confirmed, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.25">Isa 22:25</reference>. <div eID="gen27363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> This prophecy, ending with the fourteenth verse of this chapter, is entitled, "The oracle concerning the valley of vision," by which is meant Jerusalem, because, says Sal. ben Melech, it was the place of prophecy. Jerusalem, according to Josephus, was built upon two opposite hills Sion and Acra, separated by a valley in the midst. He speaks of another broad valley between Acra and Moriah, Bell. Jud. 5:13; 6:6. It was the seat of Divine revelation; the place where chiefly prophetic vision was given, and where God manifested himself visibly in the holy place. The prophecy foretells the invasion of Jerusalem by the Assyrians under Sennacherib; or by the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar. Vitringa is of opinion that the prophet has both in view: that of the Chaldeans in the first part, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.1-Isa.22.5">Isa 22:1-5</reference>, which he thinks relates to the flight of Zedekiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.4">2Kgs 25:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.5">2Kgs 25:5</reference>; and that of the Assyrians in the latter part, which agrees with the circumstances of that time, and particularly describes the preparations made by Hezekiah for the defense of the city, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.8-Isa.22.11">Isa 22:8-11</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2-2Chr.32.5">2Chr 32:2-5</reference>. - L. <div eID="gen27364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> Art - gone up to the house-tops "Are gone up to the house-tops" - The houses in the east were in ancient times, as they are still, generally, built in one and the same uniform manner. The roof or top of the house is always flat, covered with broad stones, or a strong plaster of terrace, and guarded on every side with a low parapet wall; see <reference osisRef="Deu.22.8">Deu 22:8</reference>. The terrace is frequented as much as any part of the house. On this, as the season favors, they walk, they eat, they sleep, they transact business, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.9.25">1Sam 9:25</reference>, see also the Septuagint in that place), they perform their devotions <reference osisRef="Act.10.9">Act 10:9</reference>. The house is built with a court within, into which chiefly the windows open: those that open to the street are so obstructed with lattice-work that no one either without or within can see through them. Whenever, therefore, any thing is to be seen or heard in the streets, any public spectacle, any alarm of a public nature, every one immediately goes up to the house-top to satisfy his curiosity. In the same manner, when any one has occasion to make any thing public, the readiest and most effectual way of doing it is to proclaim it from the house-tops to the people in the streets. "What ye hear in the ear, that publish ye on the house-top," saith our Savior, <reference osisRef="Mat.10.27">Mat 10:27</reference>. The people running all to the tops of their houses gives a lively image of a sudden general alarm. Sir John Chardin's MS. note on this place is as follows: "Dans les festes pour voir passer quelque chose, et dans les maladies pour les annoncer aux voisins en allumant des lumieres, le peuple monte sur les terrasses." "In festivals, in order to see what is going forward, and in times of sickness, in order to indicate them to neighbors by lighting of candles, the people go up to the house-tops."
entries.cb4d1d4519fe4cfc752b9ac10b8be32453fe5f32: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> All thy rulers - are bound by the archers "All thy leaders - are fled from the bow" - There seems to be somewhat of an inconsistency in the sense according to the present reading. If the leaders were bound, אסרו usseru, how could they flee away? for their being bound, according to the obvious construction and course of the sentence, is a circumstance prior to their flight. I therefore follow Houbigant, who reads הסרו huseru, remoti sunt, "they are gone off." גלו galu, transmigraverunt, Chaldee; which seems to confirm this emendation.
entries.c299e2d929947ed17a566d2fa9fe1e3bfe2c3ccf: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> Chariots of men "The Syriac" - It is not easy to say what רכב אדם recheb adam, a chariot of men, can mean. It seems by the form of the sentence, which consists of three members, the first and the third mentioning a particular people, that the second should do so likewise. Thus ברכב ארם ופרשים berecheb aram uparashim, "with chariots the Syrian, and with horsemen:" the similitude of the letters ד daleth and ר resh is so great, and the mistakes arising from it are so frequent, that I readily adopt the correction of Houbigant, ארם aram, Syria, instead of אדם adam, man; which seems to me extremely probable. The conjunction ו vau, and, prefixed to פרשים parashim, horsemen, seems necessary in whatever way the sentence may be taken; and it is confirmed by five MSS., (one ancient), four of De Rossi's, and two ancient of my own; one by correction of Dr. Kennicott's, and three editions. Kir was a city belonging to the Medes. The Medes were subject to the Assyrians in Hezekiah's time, (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Kgs 16:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2Kgs 17:6</reference>); and so perhaps might Elam (the Persians) likewise be, or auxiliaries to them.
entries.619ae4a1e1ddba3a687b1a08dafc8b364c6537e7: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> The armor "The arsenal" - Built by Solomon within the city, and called the house of the forest of Lebanon; probably from the great quantity of cedar from Lebanon which was employed in the building. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.2">1Kgs 7:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.3">1Kgs 7:3</reference>.
entries.807a71bb05433a50c55dedbe271ed1599945c38a: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> Ye gathered together the waters "And ye shall collect the waters" - There were two pools in or near Jerusalem, supplied by springs: the upper pool, or the old pool, supplied by the spring called Gihon, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Chr 32:30</reference>, towards the higher part of the city, near Sion, or the city of David, and the lower pool, probably supplied by Siloam, towards the lower part. When Hezekiah was threatened with a siege by Sennacherib, he stopped up all the waters of the fountains without the city; and brought them into the city by a conduit, or subterranean passage cut through the rock; those of the old pool, to the place where he had a double wall, so that the pool was between the two walls. This he did in order to distress the enemy, and to supply the city during the siege. This was so great a work that not only the historians have made particular mention of it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.20.20">2Kgs 20:20</reference>;<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.2">2Chr 32:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.3">2Chr 32:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.5">2Chr 32:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.32.30">2Chr 32:30</reference>; but the son of Sirach also has celebrated it in his encomium on Hezekiah. "Hezekiah fortified his city, and brought in water into the midst thereof: he digged the hard rock with iron, and made wells for water," Ecclesiasticus 48.
entries.e17df16816a061ba2d9ab5cda8746c9ef2d963ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27371" type="x-p"/> Unto the maker thereof "To him that hath disposed this" - That is, to God the Author and Disposer of this visitation, the invasion with which he now threatens you.
